results.key_finding: Adds the optic nerve as a fifth region and the kappa free-light-chain index as a CSF marker, and advises additional supporting evidence (spinal cord lesions, positive CSF or the central vein sign) in people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, in whom non-specific white matter lesions are common.
results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria (Montalban X et al.)

results.key_finding: Onset after 50 was more often motor and spinal, and a progressive course was more frequent than in younger-onset disease; diagnosis was often delayed.
results.title: Clinical characteristics of patients with late-onset multiple sclerosis (Kis B, Rumberg B, Berlit P)

results.key_finding: Small-vessel disease lesions are usually deep and punctate, spare the U-fibres, corpus callosum and cord, and lack central veins; ovoid periventricular, juxtacortical and short peripheral cord lesions favour MS.
results.title: The current role of MRI in differentiating multiple sclerosis from its imaging mimics (Geraldes R et al.)

output.summary: In late-onset presentations with vascular risk factors, non-specific white matter lesions are common, and the 2024 McDonald criteria advise additional supporting evidence such as spinal cord lesions or positive CSF. Lesion location and shape on brain and cord MRI help separate MS from small-vessel disease.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not attribute the white matter lesions to small-vessel disease without explaining the cord lesions, the enhancing lesions and the CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands
Do not dismiss the left eye episode as dry eye or hypertensive retinopathy: the left RAPD and disc pallor show a prior left optic neuropathy

Do not start fingolimod or another S1P modulator without a baseline ECG and first-dose heart-rate monitoring, confirmation that his sleep apnoea is treated, and an eye examination for macular oedema, which diabetes makes more likely
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord and left optic nerve, with the cord lesions and CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands as the additional evidence advised at age 54 with vascular risk).

Treat the current myelitis relapse with high-dose methylprednisolone (IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days as an inpatient, or oral 500 mg daily for 5 days) after excluding urinary infection with urinalysis and culture, with capillary glucose monitoring and correction insulin while he takes metformin, and potassium checks on hydrochlorothiazide.
Assess the new urinary urgency with a post-void residual before choosing bladder treatment.

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (three attacks in 14 months with enhancing cerebellar peduncle and cervical cord lesions favour a high-efficacy therapy), taking his diabetes-related infection risk into account.

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, screen HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV, HIV (done), VZV IgG and serum immunoglobulins, add anti-JCV antibodies if natalizumab is considered, and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting.
Optimise blood pressure (158/94 mmHg), LDL (112 mg/dL) and glycaemic control (HbA1c 7.4%) with his primary care team.
Replace vitamin D (16 ng/mL) and check methylmalonic acid for the low-normal B12 (224 pg/mL) on long-term metformin, replacing B12 if it is raised.

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure or episodic loss of awareness; the fatigue and mild cognitive slowing do not need an EEG.

A 3-week progressive myelopathy without headache, trauma or reduced consciousness: the MS-protocol MRI answers the question, and CT neither shows cord lesions nor separates demyelination from small-vessel change.
No restricted diffusion, no territorial infarct and a cord syndrome: no embolic question for which an echocardiogram would help.
No palpitations, syncope or embolic pattern; his father's atrial fibrillation does not make rhythm monitoring part of this work-up.

differential.key_features: Probably accounts for the punctate deep centrum semiovale lesions given hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia and smoking; does not explain ovoid lesions perpendicular to the ventricles, the juxtacortical and enhancing cerebellar peduncle lesions, two cord lesions, the left optic neuropathy or CSF-restricted bands.
Vascular risk; against it: progression over 3 weeks rather than sudden onset, two separate peripheral cord lesions, one enhancing, and positive CSF.
Optic neuropathy and myelitis in an older African American man; against it: AQP4-IgG negative by cell-based assay, short peripheral cord lesions, CSF-restricted bands.
MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay; ovoid periventricular lesions and CSF-restricted bands are uncommon in MOGAD.
ESR 22 with normal CRP; no infarcts or restricted diffusion, no headache or encephalopathy, CSF with restricted bands rather than a vasculitic pattern.

differential.key_features: B12 224 pg/mL with homocysteine 14.2 micromol/L on long-term metformin; against it as the cause: asymmetric syndrome, peripheral lesions in two segments with enhancement, brain lesions and CSF-restricted bands. Coexisting deficiency not excluded.
Earlier attribution to cervical radiculopathy; spine MRI shows intramedullary lesions without disc protrusion or stenosis compressing the cord.
Serum RPR and CSF VDRL non-reactive.
No leptomeningeal enhancement, CSF ACE within reference, calcium normal, no systemic features.

key_clinical_evidence: Three weeks of progressive right leg weakness with right Babinski sign, right dorsal column loss and left leg pinprick loss (a partial right hemicord pattern), Lhermitte sign and new urinary urgency; earlier right hand clumsiness and tingling for 3 weeks 14 months ago and left eye blurring for 5 days 8 months ago.

DIS: 5 of 5 regions: periventricular (ovoid lesions perpendicular to the lateral ventricles), juxtacortical (right superior frontal), infratentorial (left middle cerebellar peduncle, enhancing), spinal cord (C4-C5 enhancing, T6-T7), optic nerve (left RAPD and pallor, pRNFL 71 um, P100 131 ms).

Age 54 with hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia and 18 pack-years: the additional supporting evidence the 2024 criteria advise is present as two short peripheral cord lesions and positive CSF (six CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands, kFLC index 27.5, reference < 6.1).

The punctate deep centrum semiovale lesions are non-specific and probably reflect coexisting small-vessel disease; small-vessel disease does not explain the cord lesions, the enhancing lesions, the optic neuropathy or the CSF.
Mimics argued against: AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay; ANA, HIV, RPR and CSF VDRL negative; no cord compression.
B12 224 pg/mL with homocysteine 14.2 micromol/L on long-term metformin, and 25-OH vitamin D 16 ng/mL: deficiencies to address that do not explain the lesions or the CSF.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: a 54-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia and a smoking history presents with a partial right hemicord syndrome and Lhermitte sign, with earlier episodes misattributed to radiculopathy and hypertensive retinopathy. Vascular risk and non-specific deep white matter lesions anchor toward small-vessel disease. The agent must recognise MS-typical lesions, use the cord lesions and positive CSF as the additional evidence advised over age 50, exclude NMOSD, and plan corticosteroids around his diabetes.

patient.history_present_illness: A 54-year-old right-handed African American man with longstanding hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a significant smoking history presents to the neurology inpatient service for evaluation of progressive right leg weakness and sensory loss. He reports that approximately 3 weeks ago he noticed increasing difficulty lifting his right foot when climbing stairs and a feeling of heaviness in the right leg. Over the subsequent days, he developed numbness of the right leg from the mid-thigh down, with paresthesias that he describes as 'pins and needles.' He also reports an unusual sensation: he discovered last week that flexing his neck while looking downward produces an instantaneous electric current that shoots down his spine and into both legs, which he finds alarming. His wife has noted that he drags his right foot slightly when walking, something that was not present a month ago. He denies bowel or bladder incontinence but acknowledges some mild urinary urgency over the past two weeks. He has no weakness in the upper extremities and no diplopia or facial numbness at present. On review of prior episodes, he recalls a 3-week period approximately 14 months ago of right-hand clumsiness and tingling that resolved spontaneously and was attributed to cervical radiculopathy. He also recalls a 5-day episode of blurry vision in the left eye 8 months ago that was attributed to hypertensive retinopathy and dry eye. He is a former smoker. His father died of an ischemic stroke, and his family is worried he is having a stroke. The patient himself wonders if these represent 'small strokes' related to his blood pressure history. He works full-time as a high school principal and has been struggling with fatigue and cognitive slowing over the past several months, which he attributed to work stress and poor sleep from his sleep apnea.

neurological_exam.additional: Lhermitte sign present: flexion of the neck provokes an electrical tingling sensation radiating down the thoracic spine and into both legs. No meningismus. No papilledema.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin: mildly clumsy on right, intact left. Rapid alternating movements: mildly reduced right hand.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual acuity 20/30 left eye, 20/20 right eye. Left relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) present (grade 1). Visual fields full to confrontation. Fundoscopy: mild disc pallor left optic nerve head; right fundus normal. CN III, IV, VI: Extraocular movements intact; no nystagmus. CN V: Facial sensation intact bilaterally. CN VII: No facial asymmetry; nasolabial folds symmetric. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact. CN IX-XII: Intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Mild circumduction of right leg. Tandem gait impaired, veers right. Romberg positive (increased sway with eyes closed). Cannot walk on heels on the right.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech is fluent without dysarthria. Language: naming, repetition, and comprehension normal. Mild word-finding difficulty noted on formal testing. MMSE 27/30 (missed 1 serial-7 subtraction, 1 recall item). Mood: mildly anxious.
neurological_exam.motor: Upper extremities: 5/5 bilaterally in deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, and grip. Lower extremities: Right hip flexor 4+/5, right knee extensor 4+/5; left lower extremity 5/5. No pronator drift. Mild increased tone in right lower extremity. No fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 3+ right, 2+ left (asymmetrically brisk). Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar response: extensor (Babinski) on the right, flexor on the left.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reduced light touch over the right leg from mid-thigh to foot. Vibration reduced in the right foot (6/8 on a graduated tuning fork, left 8/8); proprioception slightly impaired at the right great toe. Pinprick and temperature reduced over the left leg from mid-thigh to foot. No sensory level on the trunk. Upper limbs normal.
